summary: Specifies the wais URI scheme, originally defined in RFC 1738. It was written so RFC 1738 could be made obsolete while keeping information about the scheme on record. This document is historic.

eli5.summary: WAIS was an old way to search for documents online. This memo just keeps a note of how its web-address style worked, as a record of the past.

subtitle: How to write addresses for searching document databases with WAIS.

tldr.problem: RFC 1738 was becoming obsolete but contained the definition of the WAIS URI scheme, which needed to remain on standards track.
tldr.mechanism: This document extracts and republishes the WAIS URI scheme specification with the same syntax and rules, allowing RFC 1738 to be obsoleted while preserving the information.
tldr.outcome: The WAIS protocol was never widely implemented and almost no WAIS servers are in use today, making this mostly a historical record.

today: RFC 4156 is Historic. The WAIS protocol was never widely implemented and almost no WAIS servers are in use today.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The WAIS URI scheme specifies how to write web addresses for WAIS databases and searches. Originally defined in RFC 1738, this document preserves the specification so it remains available on standards track after RFC 1738 was made obsolete.

The WAIS protocol is based on Z39.50-1988, a library search standard, but the WAIS URL scheme is not intended for use with arbitrary Z39.50 services.
sections.eli5: WAIS was a way to search for documents online. This memo saves the rules for writing WAIS addresses.

sections.title: WAIS URI Syntax
sections.content:
A WAIS URL takes one of three forms. The simplest, wais://<host>:<port>/<database>, designates a database available for searching. If the port is omitted, it defaults to 210.

A search URL adds a query: wais://<host>:<port>/<database>?<search>, which designates a particular search result.

The third form retrieves a specific document from the database: wais://<host>:<port>/<database>/<wtype>/<wpath>. The <wtype> identifies the object type (required because clients need to know the type before retrieving), and <wpath> is the WAIS document identifier, which is opaque and meaningful only to the server that issued it.
sections.eli5: WAIS addresses look like other web addresses. They point to a database, or to a search, or to a specific document inside a database.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The WAIS protocol offers no privacy or authentication mechanisms, as noted in RFC 1625. Standard URI security considerations, discussed in RFC 3986, also apply to WAIS URIs.
sections.eli5: WAIS does not hide messages or check who is talking to whom, so secure communication requires other safeguards.
